'''''Betonica officinalis''''', [[common name]] '''betony'''<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Betony ''Betonica officinalis'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.6yb1xg |access-date=20 July 2024 }}</ref><ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=17 October 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=David Chapman |title=Exploring the Cornish Coast |date=2008 |publisher=Alison Hodge |location=[[Penzance]] |isbn=9780906720561 |page=113 }}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the mint [[family (botany)|family]] Lamiaceae, native to Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa.<ref name=powo/> Other vernacular names include wood betony,<ref name=Culpeper/> common hedgenettle,<ref>{{PLANTS|id=STOF2|taxon=Stachys officinalis|access-date=30 November 2015 }}</ref> purple betony, bishopwort, or bishop's wort. Its 'Hummelo' cultivar has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHS_377707" >{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/377707/betonica-officinalis-hummelo/details |title=''Betonica officinalis'' 'Hummelo' |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2026 |website=Find a plant |publisher=The Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=5 April 2026 |quote=Synonyms; ''Stachys macrantha'' 'Hummelo', ''Stachys officinalis'' 'Hummelo', ''Stachys monieri'' 'Hummelo' ... 50 suppliers }}</ref>

It was until recently usually included in the genus ''[[Stachys]]'' as its [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] ''Stachys officinalis'',<ref name = "Streeter">Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0 }}</ref> but ''Betonica'' was separated at [[genus]] rank from ''Stachys'' when a detailed examination showed clear consistent differences in both the foliage and flowers, valid at a higher rank than the previous treatment as just a [[subgenus]].<ref name="Giuliani">{{cite journal |last1=Giuliani |first1=C. |last2=Maleci Bini |first2=L. |title=Glandular trichomes as further differential characters between ''Stachys'' subgenus ''Betonica'' (L.) Bhattacharjee and ''Stachys'' subgenus ''Stachys'' |journal=Plant Biosystems |date=2012 |volume=146 |issue=supplement 1 |page=1–8 |doi=10.1080/11263504.2012.663810 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/11263504.2012.663810 |access-date=20 July 2024 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This has been confirmed by genetic study, which shows ''Betonica'' is separate from ''Stachys'' and more closely related to the hemp-nettles ''[[Galeopsis]]''.<ref name="Bendiksby">{{cite journal |last1=Bendiksby |first1=Mika |last2=Thorbek |first2=Lisbeth |last3=Scheen |first3=Anne-Cathrine |last4=Lindqvist |first4=Charlotte |last5=Ryding |first5=Olof |title=An updated phylogeny and classification of Lamiaceae subfamily Lamioideae |journal=Taxon |date=2011 |volume=60 |issue=2 |page=471–484 }}</ref>

The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''[[officinalis]]'' refers to plants which had a culinary or medicinal use.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>

==Description==
''Betonica officinalis'' is a [[rhizome|rhizomatous]], patch-forming, grassland [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing to {{convert|30-60|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall. Its leaves are stalked on upright stems, narrowly oval, with a heart-shaped base, with a somewhat wrinkled texture and toothed margins. The [[sepal|calyx]] is 5–7 mm long, with 5 teeth, edged with bristles. The [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]] 1–1.5 cm long. Its upper lip flat, almost straight when seen from the side. The [[anther]]s stick straight out. It flowers in mid summer from July to September, and is found in dry grassland, [[meadow]]s and open woods in most of Europe, western Asia and North Africa.<ref> {{cite web |title=Ecological Flora of Britain & Ireland |url=http://ecoflora.org.uk/search_ecochars.php?plant_no=1510160030%20&cs=1 |access-date=19 September 2021 }}</ref><ref name = "Streeter"/> In the [[British Isles]] it is common in [[England and Wales]], but scarce in southern Scotland and rare in Ireland and northern Scotland.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020/>

The aerial parts contain [[phenylethanoid]] [[glycoside]]s betonyosides A-F, [[Verbascoside|acetoside]], acetoside isomer, campneosides II, forsythoside B, and leucosceptoside B.<ref>Miyase T., Yamamoto R., Ueno A., "Phenylethanoid glycosides from Stachys officinalis". ''Phytochemistry'' 1996 43:2 (475–479)</ref> The roots contain the [[diterpene]] glycosides betonicosides A-D and the diterpene betonicolide.<ref>Miyase T., Yamamoto R., Ueno A. ,"Betonicosides A-D and betonicolide, diterpenoids from the roots of Stachys officinalis" ''Chemical and Pharmaceutical Bulletin'' 1996 44:8 (1610–1613)</ref>

==History and uses==
[[File:De Matiera Medica Abbasid periode Bagdad 1224 kestron = Betonica officinalis.jpg|thumb|Betony in a 13th-century Arabic edition of ''[[De Materia Medica]]'']]
In his [[Natural History (Pliny)|Natural History]], [[Pliny the Elder]] claims betony was "a plant more highly esteemed than any other", and documents a popular belief that merely possessing betony would protect a house from harm. Pliny also states it was discovered by the [[Vettones]] of Spain, hence the Gaulish name for the plant, Vettonica.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pliny the Elder, The Natural History, BOOK XXV. THE NATURAL HISTORY OF WILD PLANT, CHAP. 46.—THE CESTROS, PSYCHOTROPEION, VETTONICA, OR SERRA- TULA: FORTY-EIGHT REMEDIES. |url=http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=urn:cts:latinLit:phi0978.phi001.perseus-eng1:25.46 |access-date=27 December 2023 |website=www.perseus.tufts.edu }}</ref>

''De herba Vettonica liber'', a book originally attributed to [[Antonius Musa]] but now thought to have been written in the 4th century,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Langslow |first=D. R. |title=Medical Latin in the Roman Empire |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |year=2000 |pages=67–68 |language=en }}</ref> lists nearly 50 uses for the plant. These include easing of pain and fever after childbirth, prevention of drunkenness, against snake and mad dog bites, curing of various pains, and against horrors. Pseudo-Musa also claims the herb was discovered by either the Greek god of medicine [[Asclepius|Aesculapius]] or the centaur [[Chiron]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pseudo-Musa: De herba vettonica liber |url=https://www.uni-giessen.de/de/fbz/fb05/germanistik/absprache/sprachverwendung/gloning/ch/musa-vet.htm |access-date=27 December 2023 |website=Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen |language=de }}</ref>

Information about and uses for betony are compiled in Chapter 232 of [[John Gerard]]'s 1597 ''Herball, or, Generall historie of plantes''. Properties ascribed to it include help for those with "the falling sickness", cramps, ague, jaundice, and sciatica, clearing of the lungs, chest, liver, and gallbladder, killing of worms, and breakage of kidney stones, among many others.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gerard |first=John |url=http://archive.org/details/mobot31753000817749 |title=The Herball, or, Generall historie of plantes, gathered by John Gerarde of London, master in chirurgerie. |date=1597 |publisher=Imprinted at London by John Norton |pages=577–578 }}</ref>

In his 1652 work ''The English physitian'', [[Nicholas Culpeper]] called it Wood-Betony to contrast it from Water-Betony, but noted it was also called Common Betony. He observed that "Bettony that grows in the shadow is far better than that which grows in the Sun, because it delights in the shadow".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Culpeper |first=Nicholas |url=http://archive.org/details/b30335310 |title=The English Physitian: OR An Astrologo-Physical Discourse of the Vulgar Herbs of this Nation. Being a Compleat Method of Physick... |date=1652 |publisher=Printed by P. Cole |edition=1st |location=London |pages=244 }}</ref> He mentions Antonius Musa as a source. His summary of uses for betony is vast, and reflects influence from Pseudo-Musa and the same tradition as Gerard: "''[[Epidemic|Epidemical Diseases]], [[Witchcraft]], Apetite, [[Indigestion]], Stomach, [[Burping|Belching]], [[Jaundice]], Falling-sickness, [[Palsy|Palsey]], [[Convulsion]], Shrinking of the [[Tendon|Sinews]], [[Gout]], [[Edema|Dropsie]], Frensie, Cough, [[Common cold|Cold]], Shortness of Breath, [[Fever|Agues of all sorts]], Sore Eyes, Worms, Obstructions of the Liver and Spleen, Stitches, Pains in the Back and Belly, Terms provokes, Mother, Childbirth Stone, [[Toothache]], Venemous Beasts, Mad-dogs, Weariness, Bleeding at Mouth and Nose, Pissing & spitting of Blood, Ruptures, [[Bruises]], [[Wounds]], [[Veins]] and Sinews Cut, [[Ulcer|Ulcers]], [[Fistula|Fistulaes]], [[Boil (infection)|Boyls]], Ears''." Culpeper classifies betony under the planet [[Jupiter (astrology)|Jupiter]] and the sign [[Aries (astrology)|Aries]].<ref name=Culpeper>{{Cite book |last=Culpeper |first=Nicholas |url=http://archive.org/details/b30335310 |title=The English Physitian: OR An Astrologo-Physical Discourse of the Vulgar Herbs of this Nation. Being a Compleat Method of Physick... |date=1652 |publisher=Printed by P. Cole |edition=1st |location=London |pages=14–15 }}</ref>

A Welsh prescription attributed to the [[Physicians of Myddfai]] ascribes dream-controlling properties to betony, advising hanging its leaves around the neck or drinking the juice before sleep.<ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/1256144 Bonser, Wilfrid, "Magical Practices against Elves". Folklore, Vol. 37, No. 4 (Dec. 31, 1926), pp. 350-363.]</ref>

The plant was commonly grown by monks and apothecaries for medicinal purposes, hence the [[specific epithet]] ''[[officinalis]]'' which indicates use for medicinal or culinary purposes.<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>

Betony was an ingredient of [[pistoja|Pistoia]] powder, an old remedy for arthritis and gout.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=3 April 1909 |title=Pistoia Gout Powders |journal=British Medical Journal |volume=1 |issue=2518 |pages=852 |issn=0007-1447 |pmc=2318516 |pmid=20764391 }}</ref>

Betony is among the herbs possibly used by the [[Druid|Druids]] to make wine and holy water.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=26 December 1908 |title=Literary Notes |journal=British Medical Journal |volume=2 |issue=2504 |pages=1876 |issn=0007-1447 |pmc=2438171 }}</ref>

12 [[Prairial]] in the [[French Republican calendar]] is dedicated to betony.

Betony is mentioned in Cadfael season 1, episode 1, One Corpse Too Many, as Cadfael soaks a bandage with betony to help make the wound of a wounded person knit.

Betony has also been used in traditional Austrian medicine internally as tea, or externally as compresses or baths for treatment of disorders of the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, nervous system, skin and gynecological problems.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

Modern herbalists prescribe betony to treat [[anxiety]], [[gallstone]]s, [[heartburn]], high [[blood pressure]], [[migraine]] and [[neuralgia]], and to prevent [[sweat]]ing. It can also be used as an [[ointment]] for cuts and sores.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}
